claim: Cav1.4 L-type channels are required for the formation of rod photoreceptor synapses in the retina.
source: Here, we addressed this unknown with respect to the requirement for Cav1.4 L-type channels for the formation of rod photoreceptor synapses in the retina.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as the research question being addressed.

claim: The Cav1.4 protein, but not its Ca2+ conductance, is required for the molecular assembly of rod synapses.
source: Using a mouse strain expressing a non-conducting mutant form of Cav1.4, we report that the Cav1.4 protein, but not its Ca2+ conductance, is required for the molecular assembly of rod synapses
evidence: This is the primary finding stated in the abstract based on experiments with the G369i mutant mouse.

claim: Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals are needed for the appropriate recruitment of postsynaptic partners.
source: however, Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals are needed for the appropriate recruitment of postsynaptic partners.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract based on experimental observations.

claim: The primary function of voltage-gated Cav Ca2+ channels within axon terminals is to serve as a conduit for Ca2+ ions that trigger the fusion of neurotransmitter-laden vesicles with the presynaptic membrane.
source: It is well established that the primary function of voltage-gated Cav Ca2+ channels within axon terminals is to serve as a conduit for Ca2+ ions that trigger the fusion of neurotransmitter-laden vesicles with the presynaptic membrane (reviewed in Dolphin and Lee, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Mutations in genes encoding presynaptic Cav channels cause neurological disorders such as epilepsy, migraine, and ataxia.
source: Mutations in genes encoding presynaptic Cav channels cause neurological disorders such as epilepsy, migraine, and ataxia (Pietrobon, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Neurotransmitter release has a steep Ca2+-dependence.
source: Due to the steep Ca2+-dependence of neurotransmitter release (Dodge and Rahamimoff, 1967), factors that modulate Cav channel function can dramatically alter synaptic output.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dodge and Rahamimoff, 1967.

claim: Voltage-dependent changes in the conformation of Cav1.1 channels, rather than the incoming Ca2+ ions, initiate skeletal muscle contraction.
source: For example, voltage-dependent changes in the conformation of Cav1.1 channels, rather than the incoming Ca2+ ions, initiate skeletal muscle contraction (Adams et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Adams et al., 1990.

claim: Cav1.4 is the predominant Cav subtype in rod and cone photoreceptors in the retina.
source: To overcome these hurdles, we focused on the Cav1.4 L-type channel, which is the predominant Cav subtype in rod and cone photoreceptors in the retina (Mansergh et al., 2005; Chang et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: More than 140 mutations in the human CACNA1F gene encoding Cav1.4 have been identified.
source: More than 140 mutations in the human CACNA1F gene encoding Cav1.4 have been identified, many of which cause heterogeneous forms of vision impairment (Waldner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Waldner et al., 2018.

claim: The absence of photoreceptor synaptic responses in Cav1.4 KO mice has been attributed to a requirement for Cav1.4 in the presynaptic release of glutamate.
source: The absence of photoreceptor synaptic responses in Cav1.4 KO mice has been attributed to a requirement for Cav1.4 in the presynaptic release of glutamate (Mansergh et al., 2005; Chang et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Photoreceptor synapses do not form in Cav1.4 KO mice.
source: However, an additional contributing factor is that photoreceptor synapses do not form in Cav1.4 KO mice (Liu et al., 2013; Zabouri and Haverkamp, 2013; Regus-Leidig et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Rod and cone photoreceptors communicate visual information via a triadic 'ribbon' synapse containing postsynaptic neurites of a depolarizing (ON) bipolar cell and two horizontal cells (HCs).
source: Rod and cone photoreceptors communicate visual information via a triadic 'ribbon' synapse containing postsynaptic neurites of a depolarizing (ON) bipolar cell and two horizontal cells (HCs) (Masland, 2012; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: During the first postnatal week in mice, ribbons develop from spherical precursors and are concentrated in the outer plexiform layer (OPL) where mature rod and cone synapses are localized.
source: During the first postnatal week in mice, ribbons develop from spherical precursors and are concentrated in the outer plexiform layer (OPL) where mature rod and cone synapses are localized (Blanks et al., 1974; Regus-Leidig et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to developmental studies.

claim: In Cav1.4 KO mice, spheres, rather than ribbons, are present at all developmental ages and often found in the outer nuclear layer (ONL).
source: In Cav1.4 KO mice, the development of these synapses appears stunted in that spheres, rather than ribbons, are present at all developmental ages and often found in the outer nuclear layer (ONL) that normally contains only photoreceptor somas.
evidence: This is a description of the phenotype observed in Cav1.4 KO mice.

claim: The terminals of rods and cones of Cav1.4 KO mice are misshapen.
source: The terminals of rods and cones (i.e., spherules and pedicles, respectively) (Figure 1A) of Cav1.4 KO mice are misshapen, and a number of proteins typical of mature synapses are absent or aberrantly localized (Raven et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2013; Zabouri and Haverkamp, 2013; Regus-Leidig et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: A number of proteins typical of mature synapses are absent or aberrantly localized in Cav1.4 KO mice.
source: The terminals of rods and cones (i.e., spherules and pedicles, respectively) (Figure 1A) of Cav1.4 KO mice are misshapen, and a number of proteins typical of mature synapses are absent or aberrantly localized (Raven et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2013; Zabouri and Haverkamp, 2013; Regus-Leidig et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The G369i mutation in Cav1.3 results in the insertion of a glycine residue into transmembrane segment 6 of domain I and prevents Ca2+ influx through the channel during membrane depolarizations.
source: The mutation results in the insertion of a glycine residue into transmembrane segment 6 of domain I (G369i, Figure 1B) and prevents Ca2+ influx through the channel during membrane depolarizations (Baig et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Baig et al., 2011 and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: β2 and α2δ−4 subunits are the major Cav auxiliary subunits forming Cav1.4 complexes in photoreceptor synaptic terminals.
source: The wild-type (WT) and G369i mutant channels were co-expressed with β2 and α2δ−4 subunits which are the major Cav auxiliary subunits forming Cav1.4 complexes in photoreceptor synaptic terminals (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2015.

claim: G369i mutant Cav1.4 channels were associated with the plasma membrane but did not mediate significant inward Ba2+ currents like WT channels.
source: G369i mutant channels were associated with the plasma membrane but did not mediate significant inward Ba2+ currents (IBa) like WT channels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Peak IBa densities mediated by WT Cav1.4 channels were −20.70 ± 5.31 pA/pF.
source: Compared to robust peak IBa densities mediated by WT channels (−20.70 ± 5.31 pA/pF), those in cells transfected with G369i mutant channels were negligible (−1.14 ± 0.11 pA/pF, p=0.03)
evidence: This is experimental data from patch clamp recordings.

claim: Peak IBa densities in cells transfected with G369i mutant Cav1.4 channels were −1.14 ± 0.11 pA/pF.
source: Compared to robust peak IBa densities mediated by WT channels (−20.70 ± 5.31 pA/pF), those in cells transfected with G369i mutant channels were negligible (−1.14 ± 0.11 pA/pF, p=0.03)
evidence: This is experimental data from patch clamp recordings.

claim: Peak IBa densities in cells transfected with G369i mutant Cav1.4 channels were not significantly different from cells transfected only with β2 and α2δ−1 as negative controls.
source: those in cells transfected with G369i mutant channels were negligible (−1.14 ± 0.11 pA/pF, p=0.03) and not significantly different from that in cells transfected only with β2 and α2δ−1 as negative controls (−0.56 ± 0.15 pA/pF, p=0.72, by Kruskal-Wallis test and post-hoc Dunn's test; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Gating currents were evident for both WT and G369i mutant Cav1.4 channels, but not in negative control cells.
source: Igating was evident for both WT and G369i mutant channels, but not in the negative control cells.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from electrophysiology recordings.

claim: Qmax did not differ for WT (4.22 ± 1.34 fC/pF) and G369i mutant Cav1.4 channels (3.22 ± 0.48 fC/pF, p=0.57).
source: When normalized to cell size, Qmax did not differ for WT (4.22 ± 1.34 fC/pF) and G369i mutant channels (3.22 ± 0.48 fC/pF, p=0.57 by unpaired t-test; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: G369i prevents Ca2+ conductance but not cell-surface trafficking or voltage-sensor movements in Cav1.4.
source: Thus, G369i prevents Ca2+ conductance but not cell-surface trafficking or voltage-sensor movements in Cav1.4.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on gating currents and surface expression.

claim: Inward currents such as those measured in rods of WT mice were not evident in rods of G369i KI mice.
source: In agreement with our findings in the heterologous expression system, inward currents such as those measured in rods of WT mice, were not evident in those of the knock-in mouse strain (G369i KI).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from patch clamp recordings in retinal slices.

claim: The absence of depolarization-evoked currents was similar in G369i KI mice and Cav1.4 KO mice.
source: The absence of depolarization-evoked currents was similar in G369i KI mice and a mouse strain completely lacking Cav1.4 expression (Cav1.4 KO, Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Cav1.4 protein was detected in retinal lysates of G369i KI mice by Western blot.
source: However, Cav1.4 protein was detected in retinal lysates of G369i KI mice by Western blot (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Immunofluorescence corresponding to G369i mutant channels was abundant in the OPL and juxtaposed near the ribbon as in WT mouse retina.
source: Moreover, immunofluorescence corresponding to G369i mutant channels was abundant in the OPL, where photoreceptor synapses normally form, and juxtaposed near the ribbon as in WT mouse retina (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The G369i mutant channel is expressed and targeted appropriately in photoreceptors of G369i KI mice.
source: Therefore, while it does not mediate voltage-dependent Ca2+ currents, the G369i mutant channel is expressed and targeted appropriately in photoreceptors of G369i KI mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on Western blot and immunofluorescence data.

claim: ERGs of dark-adapted G369i KI mice lacked b-waves at all but the highest light intensities.
source: Electroretinograms (ERGs) of dark-adapted G369i KI mice lacked b-waves at all but the highest light intensities, consistent with a disruption of rod synaptic transmission (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is based on ERG data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: A-waves were not significantly different in WT and G369i KI mice.
source: A-waves, which represent light-dependent hyperpolarization of photoreceptors, were not significantly different in WT and G369i KI mice (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is based on ERG data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: G369i KI mice show defects in photoreceptor function that are largely restricted to synaptic terminals.
source: Thus, G369i KI mice show defects in photoreceptor function that are largely restricted to synaptic terminals.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ERG data showing normal a-waves but disrupted b-waves.

claim: Rod synapses are more severely disrupted than cone synapses when the presynaptic abundance of Cav1.4 is compromised.
source: Furthermore, rod synapses are more severely disrupted than cone synapses when the presynaptic abundance of Cav1.4 is compromised (Ball et al., 2002; Katiyar et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017; Kerov et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Arc-shaped ribbons were plentiful in the OPL of G369i retina.
source: While shorter on average than in WT retina, arc-shaped ribbons were plentiful in the OPL of G369i retina (Figure 2B–D)
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Ribbons in G369i KI retina were shorter on average than in WT retina.
source: While shorter on average than in WT retina, arc-shaped ribbons were plentiful in the OPL of G369i retina (Figure 2B–D)
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of ribbon lengths shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Ribbons in G369i KI retina co-clustered with proteins characteristic of mature rod synapses such as PSD-95 and β-dystroglycan.
source: arc-shaped ribbons were plentiful in the OPL of G369i retina (Figure 2B–D) and co-clustered with proteins characteristic of mature rod synapses (Figure 2E) such as PSD-95 and β-dystroglycan (Koulen et al., 1998; Blank et al., 1997)
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: PSD-95 and β-dystroglycan were undetectable in the OPL of Cav1.4 KO retina.
source: such as PSD-95 and β-dystroglycan (Koulen et al., 1998; Blank et al., 1997), which were undetectable in the OPL of Cav1.4 KO retina (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: Bassoon was tightly clustered with ribbons in G369i KI as in WT retina.
source: Bassoon, a protein involved in ribbon morphogenesis (tom Dieck et al., 2005), and RIM2, a protein implicated in regulating Cav1.4 at rod synapses (Grabner et al., 2015), were tightly clustered with ribbons in G369i KI as in WT retina (Figure 2H,I).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2H,I.

claim: RIM2 was tightly clustered with ribbons in G369i KI as in WT retina.
source: Bassoon, a protein involved in ribbon morphogenesis (tom Dieck et al., 2005), and RIM2, a protein implicated in regulating Cav1.4 at rod synapses (Grabner et al., 2015), were tightly clustered with ribbons in G369i KI as in WT retina (Figure 2H,I).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2H,I.

claim: The presynaptic assembly of rod synapses can proceed without Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals.
source: Thus, although leading to shorter ribbons, the presynaptic assembly of rod synapses can proceed without Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that ribbons and presynaptic proteins are present in G369i KI retina.

claim: At the depolarized voltage of photoreceptors in darkness, Cav1.4-dependent glutamate release activates mGluR6, which suppresses the activity of TRPM1-dependent channels.
source: At the depolarized voltage of photoreceptors in darkness, Cav1.4-dependent glutamate release activates a metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR6), which suppresses the activity of TRPM1-dependent channels (Shiells et al., 1981; Shen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations describing the signaling pathway.

claim: mGluR6 was clustered postsynaptic to rod ribbons in WT retina.
source: In agreement with previous work (Koike et al., 2010), mGluR6 was clustered postsynaptic to rod ribbons, and TRPM1 was situated at the tips of RBC dendrites in WT retina (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: TRPM1 was situated at the tips of RBC dendrites in WT retina.
source: In agreement with previous work (Koike et al., 2010), mGluR6 was clustered postsynaptic to rod ribbons, and TRPM1 was situated at the tips of RBC dendrites in WT retina (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: Arc-shaped ribbons in apposition to colocalized TRPM1 and mGluR6 could clearly be distinguished in G369i KI retina but not in Cav1.4 KO retina.
source: Although the subcellular distribution of the postsynaptic proteins was partially obscured by the diffuse pattern of TRPM1 labeling, arc-shaped ribbons in apposition to colocalized TRPM1 and mGluR6 could clearly be distinguished in G369i KI retina but not in Cav1.4 KO retina (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: The CPPG-evoked EPSC was robust and outwardly rectifying in WT RBCs.
source: As expected (Morgans et al., 2009; Shen et al., 2009), the CPPG-evoked EPSC was robust and outwardly rectifying in WT RBCs (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: The CPPG-evoked EPSC was significantly lower in amplitude in G369i KI RBCs compared to WT RBCs.
source: Although significantly lower in amplitude compared to WT RBCs, this EPSC was measurable in all RBCs that were recorded in G369i KI mice but was never detected in any of the RBC recordings in Cav1.4 KO mice (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: The CPPG-evoked EPSC was never detected in any of the RBC recordings in Cav1.4 KO mice.
source: Although significantly lower in amplitude compared to WT RBCs, this EPSC was measurable in all RBCs that were recorded in G369i KI mice but was never detected in any of the RBC recordings in Cav1.4 KO mice (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: The molecular components of the postsynaptic signaling complex in RBCs can be assembled in the absence of Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals, albeit less efficiently than in their presence.
source: These results indicate that the molecular components of the postsynaptic signaling complex in RBCs can be assembled in the absence of Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals, albeit less efficiently than in their presence.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the immunofluorescence and electrophysiology data.

claim: Sprouting of HC and RBC neurites out of the OPL and into the ONL occurs as a result of presynaptic functional impairments in rods and cones.
source: Sprouting of HC and RBC neurites out of the OPL and into the ONL, and the appearance of ectopic ribbons and other presynaptic proteins in the ONL, occurs as a result of presynaptic functional impairments in rods and cones (McCall and Gregg, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McCall and Gregg, 2008.

claim: The prevailing view has been that synaptic transmission is needed to maintain the laminar organization of photoreceptor synapses in the OPL.
source: Thus, the prevailing view has been that synaptic transmission is needed to maintain the laminar organization of photoreceptor synapses in the OPL.
evidence: This is a statement about the existing understanding in the field.

claim: HC and RBC sprouting are particularly prominent in Cav1.4 KO mice.
source: Consistent with this notion, HC and RBC sprouting (Figure 4A) are particularly prominent in Cav1.4 KO mice, which lack evidence of photoreceptor transmission (Chang et al., 2006; Raven et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2013; Zabouri and Haverkamp, 2013).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A and supported by citations.

claim: HC and RBC neurite sprouting was less prominent in G369i KI mice than in Cav1.4 KO mice.
source: Contrary to this prediction, HC and RBC neurite sprouting was less prominent in G369i KI mice than in Cav1.4 KO mice (Figure 4A,B)
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Most of the synapses in G369i KI mice were situated normally in the OPL.
source: HC and RBC neurite sprouting was less prominent in G369i KI mice than in Cav1.4 KO mice (Figure 4A,B) with most of the synapses situated normally in the OPL (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals and/or glutamatergic transmission play a supporting, but non-essential, role for the proper lamination of rod synapses within the OPL.
source: These results indicate a supporting, but non-essential, role for Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals and/or glutamatergic transmission for the proper lamination of rod synapses within the OPL.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that sprouting is reduced but not eliminated in G369i KI mice.

claim: Ribeye-labeled structures in the ONL of G369i KI mice exhibited mature ribbon morphology.
source: Compared to the spherical appearance of ribeye-labeled structures in the OPL/ONL of Cav1.4 KO and other mouse strains with presynaptic dysfunction (Chang et al., 2006; McCall and Gregg, 2008; Raven et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2013; Zabouri and Haverkamp, 2013), those in the ONL of G369i KI mice exhibited mature ribbon morphology and were associated with synaptic proteins as in the WT OPL (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Ribeye-labeled structures in the ONL of G369i KI mice were associated with synaptic proteins as in the WT OPL.
source: Compared to the spherical appearance of ribeye-labeled structures in the OPL/ONL of Cav1.4 KO and other mouse strains with presynaptic dysfunction (Chang et al., 2006; McCall and Gregg, 2008; Raven et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2013; Zabouri and Haverkamp, 2013), those in the ONL of G369i KI mice exhibited mature ribbon morphology and were associated with synaptic proteins as in the WT OPL (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Each of the four rod terminals sampled from G369i KI retina had a single ribbon that was anchored at the presynaptic membrane and was apposed to a triad of postsynaptic partners.
source: Each of the four rod terminals sampled from G369i KI retina had a single ribbon that was anchored at the presynaptic membrane and was apposed to a triad of postsynaptic partners (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from serial block-face scanning electron microscopy shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: Three of the four spherules analyzed in G369i KI retina contained more than one ribbon.
source: First, three of the four spherules that were analyzed contained more than one ribbon, rather than the single ribbon characteristic of rod terminals in the WT mouse retina (Blanks et al., 1974; Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from serial block-face scanning electron microscopy shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: Some ribbons in G369i KI rod spherules appeared club-shaped.
source: Second, some ribbons appeared club-shaped (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: At least one of the extraneous ribbons in G369i KI rod spherules was 'floating' rather than anchored near the presynaptic membrane.
source: Third, at least one of the extraneous ribbons was 'floating' rather than anchored near the presynaptic membrane.
evidence: This is based on observations from 3D reconstructions.

claim: Alterations of ribbon architecture in G369i KI rod spherules resemble the types of ribbon plasticity caused by reductions in presynaptic Ca2+ in mouse rods due to light or Ca2+ chelators.
source: These alterations of ribbon architecture in G369i KI rod spherules resemble the types of ribbon plasticity caused by reductions in presynaptic Ca2+ in mouse rods due to light or Ca2+ chelators (Spiwoks-Becker et al., 2004; Dembla et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on ribbon plasticity.

claim: The lack of Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals in G369i KI rods could have caused fragmentation of the anchored ribbon, leading to the appearance of additional short, floating ribbons.
source: Thus, the lack of Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals in G369i KI rods could have caused fragmentation of the anchored ribbon, leading to the appearance of additional short, floating ribbons.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed ribbon phenotype.

claim: Within the invagination of mouse rod spherules are normally two HC neurites and an intervening RBC neurite.
source: Normally, within the invagination of mouse rod spherules are two HC neurites and an intervening RBC neurite (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4E and represents established knowledge.

claim: The RBC neurite tip and the resident mGluR6 receptors are maintained relatively distant—hundreds of nanometers—from the release site in WT rod spherules.
source: Compared to HCs, the RBC neurite tip and the resident mGluR6 receptors are maintained relatively distant—hundreds of nanometers—from the release site (Rao-Mirotznik et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rao-Mirotznik et al., 1995.

claim: The complex organization of the rod triad is thought to be critical for controlling glutamate release volume and spillover dynamics.
source: This complex organization is thought to be critical for controlling glutamate release volume and spillover dynamics, allowing for differential activation of distinct glutamate receptor populations (Petralia et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Petralia et al., 2018.

claim: For spherules in the OPL as well as in the ONL of G369i KI retina, branching neurites of HCs and RBCs formed non-invaginating triadic contacts close to the anchored presynaptic ribbon.
source: For spherules in the OPL as well as in the ONL of G369i KI retina, branching neurites of HCs and RBCs formed non-invaginating triadic contacts close to the anchored presynaptic ribbon (Figure 4F,G), rather than invading rod spherules as in WT retina (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from serial block-face scanning electron microscopy shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: Immunolabeling for mGluR6 remained clustered near ribbons in G369i KI retina.
source: Nevertheless, immunolabeling for mGluR6 remained clustered near ribbons in G369i KI retina (Figure 3B; Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pre and postsynaptic apposition is maintained in G369i KI retina even in the absence of the normal spacing between RBC tips and the release sites.
source: Nevertheless, immunolabeling for mGluR6 remained clustered near ribbons in G369i KI retina (Figure 3B; Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that pre and postsynaptic apposition is maintained even in the absence of the normal spacing between RBC tips and the release sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunofluorescence data.

claim: mGluR6 labeling was significantly closer to that for ribbons in G369i KI than in WT retina.
source: In agreement with these findings, mGluR6 labeling was significantly closer to that for ribbons in G369i KI than in WT retina as revealed by nearest-neighbor analyses (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals are dispensable for postsynaptic partner selection at rod synapses.
source: Thus, while dispensable for postsynaptic partner selection at rod synapses, Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals are required for the invaginating arrangement of the corresponding neurites within the rod spherule and their proximity to release sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that triadic contacts form in G369i KI retina.

claim: Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals are required for the invaginating arrangement of the corresponding neurites within the rod spherule and their proximity to release sites.
source: Thus, while dispensable for postsynaptic partner selection at rod synapses, Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals are required for the invaginating arrangement of the corresponding neurites within the rod spherule and their proximity to release sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that neurites do not invaginate in G369i KI retina.

claim: Cav1.4 is expected to interact directly or indirectly with a diverse array of proteins.
source: Like other presynaptic Cav channels, Cav1.4 is expected to interact directly or indirectly with a diverse array of proteins (Dolphin and Lee, 2020), some of which are required for ribbon formation in photoreceptors (tom Dieck et al., 2005; Kiyonaka et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The Cav1.4 complex could act as a central scaffold for protein interactions that drive the assembly of the ribbon and associated components of the active zone.
source: Thus, the Cav1.4 complex could act as a central scaffold for protein interactions that drive the assembly of the ribbon and associated components of the active zone.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: Voltage-dependent conformational changes in the Cav1.4 protein are intact in G369i mutant channels.
source: Alternatively, but not mutually exclusively, voltage-dependent conformational changes in the Cav1.4 protein, which are intact in G369i mutant channels (Figure 1C), could be involved.
evidence: This is based on the gating current data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cav1.4 could conformationally couple to intracellular Ca2+ release channels, which could represent a Ca2+ source that aids presynaptic development.
source: For example, Cav1.4 could conformationally couple to intracellular Ca2+ release channels, as Cav1.1 does in skeletal muscle (Adams et al., 1990), which could represent a Ca2+ source that aids presynaptic development.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on analogy to Cav1.1.

claim: Cav1.4 appears to be expressed in bipolar cells and at much lower levels in other cell-types in mouse retina.
source: In addition to photoreceptors, Cav1.4 appears to be expressed in bipolar cells and at much lower levels in other cell-types in mouse retina (Yan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yan et al., 2020.

claim: Specific immunoreactivity for Cav1.4 in the outer retina is limited to photoreceptor terminals.
source: Because we find specific immunoreactivity for Cav1.4 in the outer retina to be limited to photoreceptor terminals (Liu et al., 2013), we favor the interpretation that Cav1.4 protein is not present to any large extent within bipolar cell soma or dendrites
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data from Liu et al., 2013.

claim: The postsynaptic structural defects of G369i KI rod synapses result primarily from the absence of presynaptic Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals in rods.
source: we favor the interpretation that Cav1.4 protein is not present to any large extent within bipolar cell soma or dendrites and that the postsynaptic structural defects of G369i KI rod synapses result primarily from the absence of presynaptic Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals in rods.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the localization of Cav1.4 expression.

claim: Presynaptic Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals could strengthen trans-synaptic signaling via cell-adhesion molecules such as NGL-2 in HCs and ELFN1 and pikachurin in RBCs.
source: In addition to supporting glutamatergic transmission, presynaptic Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals could strengthen trans-synaptic signaling via cell-adhesion molecules such as NGL-2 in HCs (Soto et al., 2013) and ELFN1 and pikachurin in RBCs (Sato et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2017), which collectively enable the invagination of the corresponding neurites into the rod terminal.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals may regulate the activities of Ca2+ sensitive proteins such as GCAP2, which binds to Ribeye and controls ribbon stability in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
source: Considering that rod ribbons are shorter in G369i KI than in WT retina (Figure 2B), Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals may also regulate the activities of Ca2+ sensitive proteins such as GCAP2, which binds to Ribeye and controls ribbon stability in a Ca2+-dependent manner (Schmitz, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by a citation to Schmitz, 2014.

claim: β2 KO and α2δ−4 KO mice exhibit severely diminished Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals.
source: Cavβ and α2δ subunits are known to facilitate the forward trafficking and maintenance of Cav channels in the plasma membrane (Dolphin and Lee, 2020). Thus, it is not surprising that β2 KO and α2δ−4 KO mice exhibit severely diminished Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge.
